reference: Ahuja, R. K., Magnanti, T. L., & Orlin, J. B. (1993). Network Flows: Theory, Algorithms, and Applications.
math_formula:
### Mathematical Model
Let N be network nodes and A be directed links. Each node k has exogenous supply s_k, exogenous demand d_k, and throughput capacity U_k. Each directed link (i,j) has cost c_{i,j} and capacity u_{i,j}.

Decision variable:
- x_{i,j} >= 0: shipment amount on directed link (i,j).

Objective:
minimize sum_{(i,j) in A} c_{i,j} x_{i,j}.

Constraints:
- s_k + sum_{(i,k) in A} x_{i,k} = d_k + sum_{(k,j) in A} x_{k,j} for every node k.
- 0 <= x_{i,j} <= u_{i,j} for every directed link (i,j).
- s_k + sum_{(i,k) in A} x_{i,k} <= U_k for every node k.

This is a continuous minimum-cost flow model. It does not include binary link activation or fixed-charge lane opening costs.
natural_language_example: A logistics network must route required shipments through a sparse set of directed lanes at minimum transportation cost. Each node may have supply, demand, and a maximum throughput capacity. Each lane has a per-unit shipping cost and a hard capacity. The planner chooses continuous nonnegative shipment quantities on the listed directed lanes so that node flow balance holds exactly, lane capacities are respected, node throughput limits are respected, and total shipping cost is minimized. This is not vehicle routing, maximum-flow path selection, or fixed-charge lane activation.
